newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton--Prices seen up in India, mixed in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Cotton--Prices seen up in India, mixed in Pakistan.

text.p: Cotton prices could firm in India next week on higher buying by state-owned agencies and stay mixed in Pakistan where funds are scarce, dealers said on Thursday.
Indian cotton prices strengthened in the past week as state-owned agencies increased buying.
"Mill buying remained at a low ebb, but increased buying by state-owned agencies, particularly the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI), dragged prices upward," one dealer said.
New crop arrivals dropped as farmers held back stocks due to lower prices, he said.

"Daily arrivals in the Punjab region dropped to 20-25,000 170-kg bales against an earlier average of 30-35,000 bales," one broker said. "Severe cold weather and unseasonal rain in some producing centres also curtailed arrivals."
In spot deals, Bengal-deshi rose 20-25 rupees to 825-855 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) while Punjab saw-ginned climbed 35-45 rupees to 1,410-1,650 rupees per maund.
Punjab F-414 rose 55-60 rupees to 1,840-1,855 rupees per maund, traders said.

They said farmers in southern India had threatened to agitate against lower cotton prices, demanding free export of cotton. "This move by the growers induced the government to order the CCI to increase buying," a dealer said.
Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) was steady at 16,500-17,500 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) for the average variety and 18,000-18,500 rupees for the superior variety, traders said.

In Pakistan, prices were likely to remain mixed on several factors, including an expected shortfall of about one million 375-lb ginned bales due to a bad crop, the absence of exporters owing to high prices and low buying interest by textile mills because of a paucity of funds, dealers said.
Textile mills had no funds to buy cotton on credit, having already utilised sanctioned loans, said Maqbool Sadiq, chairman of the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA).
The loans were authorised on the basis of 1,600 rupees per maund last year, but with prices now at 2,600 rupees the mills had used up their credit lines, he added.
Cotton prices, which had been easing in the last few days, rose sharply on higher exports of yarn at a good price, broker Nasim Usman said.
Government officials estimate 1996/97 (July-June) ex-farm cotton output will reach 9.3 million bales, including 7.2 million in Punjab province and about 2.1 million in Sindh province.
One official said production of ginned cotton was likely to be about 9.0 million bales.

A government committee that met in Multan on Tuesday noted that the area sown under cotton in 1996/97 was 3.14 million hectares against 3.0 million last year, an increase of about 4.9 percent, or eight percent more than targeted.
Cotton arrivals at ginneries had reached 7.4 million bales by January 2 against 7.7 million a year ago, an official said.
Arrivals in Punjab totalled 5.6 million bales against 6.3 million last year, and in Sindh 1.8 million against 1.4 million, he added.
Mills had bought 5.5 million bales of ginned cotton, compared to 5.3 million in the year-ago period. Ginneries had unsold stocks of 1.9 million, compared to 1.7 million last year.

The main reason for the unsold stocks was the credit squeeze from the beginning of December. The mills had no funds to purchase cotton from the ginners, who were also short of money needed to buy raw cotton from farmers, the official said.
Cotton picking was in progress in some areas, he said, adding that some big farmers were holding back stocks in the hope of getting higher prices.
In the kerb market, the rate for MNH-93 ranged between 2,590 and 2,610 rupees per maund, one broker said.
